analysis.one_liner: Caps Medicare coinsurance for outpatient surgery at the inpatient hospital deductible.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to cap Medicare copays at surgical centers was introduced in May 2025 and has sat in the Finance Committee ever since, with one cosponsor and no action taken.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare normally makes beneficiaries pay 20% of the cost of surgery done at an ambulatory surgical center (an outpatient surgery facility), and for expensive procedures that 20% share can be larger than the deductible for an entire hospital stay. This bill caps that outpatient coinsurance at the inpatient hospital deductible amount, so a patient never owes more in copays for surgery at a surgical center than they would owe a hospital. The government pays providers the difference, so facilities lose no revenue. The change would apply to services starting January 1, 2026.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who need surgery at an ambulatory surgical center and would otherwise owe coinsurance bigger than the inpatient hospital deductible — for costly procedures, the standard 20% share can run well over a thousand dollars. Ambulatory surgical centers also come out ahead, because Medicare pays them the difference between the capped copay and the full amount, so they lose no income and patients face one less reason to delay or avoid surgery.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the coinsurance Medicare beneficiaries owe for surgical facility services at an ambulatory surgical center so it never exceeds the inpatient hospital deductible for that year.

Requires Medicare to pay the surgical center the amount of the reduction, so providers are made whole and patients get relief without facilities dropping Medicare patients or shifting costs elsewhere.
Applies to all services furnished on or after January 1, 2026, so relief would start the following year.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government — and ultimately taxpayers — covers the gap between the capped copay and the full 20% coinsurance by paying surgical centers the difference, which adds to Medicare spending.

drawbacks.text: The cap is paid for with new federal spending: whenever a patient's coinsurance would have exceeded the deductible, Medicare must pay the surgical center the difference, which adds to program costs.

The fix is narrow. It only touches coinsurance for facility services at ambulatory surgical centers; it does nothing about the broader 20% coinsurance burden Medicare beneficiaries face for many other outpatient services, and using the inpatient deductible as the ceiling is an arbitrary benchmark rather than a principled limit.

By lowering what patients pay at surgical centers while hospitals are unaffected, the bill could modestly encourage more procedures to move to ambulatory centers, shifting volume and revenue between provider settings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a modest, well-targeted consumer fix: it protects Medicare patients from a genuine quirk where an outpatient surgery can cost more in coinsurance than a hospital stay would cost in deductible, and the fiscal exposure is limited because the cap only binds in cases where the 20% share exceeds the deductible. The honest objections are that it adds federal Medicare spending and that it is a narrow patch — it helps people at surgical centers while leaving the rest of Medicare's coinsurance structure untouched.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in May 2025 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a vote, or any further action.

narrative.text: Senator Bill Cassidy introduced the Medicare Beneficiary Co-Pay Fairness Act on May 15, 2025, joined by Senator Richard Blumenthal.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, the committee with jurisdiction over Medicare.
No further action has been taken since the referral: no committee vote, no floor debate, and no amendment has been recorded.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained from the outcome yet, because nothing has happened. In the meantime, Medicare beneficiaries facing outsized surgical-center copays keep paying them, and surgical centers keep collecting the full coinsurance from patients.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the status quo holds

for.name: Bill Cassidy
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-LA), sponsor; member of the Senate Finance Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap Medicare coinsurance for ambulatory surgical center services and steered it to the Finance Committee, on which he sits.

for.name: Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor at introduction, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has one Republican sponsor (Cassidy) and one Democratic cosponsor (Blumenthal), and no opposition has appeared on the record — though no vote has occurred either.

industries.note: The bill keeps these facilities fully paid: when a patient's coinsurance is capped, Medicare pays the center the difference, so facilities lose no revenue while their patients' bills shrink. Their financial interest in this bill runs alongside beneficiaries' interest in lower copays.

Making surgery at ambulatory centers cheaper for patients could shift some procedures and revenue away from hospital outpatient settings, though the bill leaves hospital charges untouched. The bill uses the hospital inpatient deductible only as a benchmark for the cap, not as a change to hospital payment.

analysis.trajectory: With a single cosponsor, no committee action in months, and hundreds of bills competing for the Finance Committee's limited calendar, the likely path is the usual one for a solo bipartisan Medicare bill: it sits in committee unless its provisions get folded into a larger Medicare or end-of-year health package. If neither happens before the 119th Congress ends in January 2027, the bill dies and would need to be reintroduced.
